title: Qakbot to Black Basta Intrusion Chain: Rapid Domain Compromise, DNS Sabotage, and Double-Extortion Ransomware
source: Cybereason Nocturnus / Global SOC & Trend Micro Research
named_stages: Stage 1: Initial Access via Thread-Hijacked Phishing and Malicious Disk Images
Stage 2: Qakbot Execution, Process Injection, and Local Persistence
Stage 3: Automated Host Discovery and Active Directory Reconnaissance
Stage 4: Secondary C2 Staging via Cobalt Strike Beacon and Brute Ratel Badger
Stage 5: Credential Dumping and Rapid Lateral Movement to Domain Controllers
Stage 6: Environmental Sabotage, Defense Impairment, and DNS Service Disruption
Stage 7: Data Exfiltration and Enterprise-Wide Black Basta Ransomware Deployment

stages.stage_name: Initial Access via Thread-Hijacked Phishing and Malicious Disk Images
stages.description: The intrusion begins with spear-phishing emails inserted into existing legitimate email threads (thread hijacking) to establish trust. The emails include links directing victims to password-protected ZIP archives containing disk images (ISO/IMG) or malicious HTML smuggling files designed to bypass Mark-of-the-Web (MotW) inspection and secure email gateways.
key_techniques: T1553.005 - Subversion of Stream Attributes: Mark-of-the-Web Bypass
stages.procedures: Victim receives an email appearing as a reply in an active correspondence thread. The lure prompts the user to download and open a password-protected ZIP containing an ISO or IMG image. When mounted by Windows, the user double-clicks a disguised LNK shortcut that executes cmd.exe or PowerShell to extract and execute an initial Qakbot loader DLL.
stages.infrastructure_c2: Compromised third-party WordPress sites, Microsoft OneDrive/SharePoint, or attacker-controlled download staging servers.

stages.stage_name: Qakbot Execution, Process Injection, and Local Persistence
stages.description: The Qakbot loader DLL executes via system binaries, performs anti-analysis checks, decrypts embedded configuration and botnet IDs, injects its core banking trojan module into legitimate Windows binaries, and establishes local persistence.
key_techniques: T1218.011 - System Binary Proxy Execution: Rundll32
T1055.001 - Process Injection: Dynamic-link Library Injection
T1547.001 - Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
T1071.001 - Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
stages.procedures: The loader executes using `rundll32.exe [malicious_dll],Wind` or `DllRegisterServer`. Qakbot unpacks in memory and injects its core DLL into benign native processes such as `wermgr.exe`, `explorer.exe`, or `mobsync.exe`. Local persistence is established via scheduled tasks created with `schtasks.exe /create /tn ...` and registry keys under `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run`.
stages.infrastructure_c2: Multi-tier Qakbot botnet infrastructure utilizing encrypted command-and-control over TLS on TCP ports 443, 995, 2222, and 32100.

stages.stage_name: Automated Host Discovery and Active Directory Reconnaissance
stages.description: Immediately following injection, Qakbot and hands-on-keyboard operators execute automated discovery commands and deploy reconnaissance utilities to identify host privileges, domain controllers, domain trust relationships, and administrative groups.
key_techniques: T1069.002 - Permission Groups Discovery: Domain Groups
stages.procedures: Operators issue command-line discovery commands: `whoami /all`, `ipconfig /all`, `arp -a`, `route print`, `net view`, `net group "Domain Admins" /domain`, `net localgroup administrators`, and `nltest /dclist:<domain>`. AdFind (`AdFind.exe -f "(objectcategory=person)"`) is dropped and executed to comprehensively extract Active Directory structures and user objects.
stages.infrastructure_c2: Interactive shell commands tunneled back through established Qakbot C2 channels.

stages.stage_name: Secondary C2 Staging via Cobalt Strike Beacon and Brute Ratel Badger
stages.description: Once network viability is confirmed, the threat actors drop high-capability commercial and adversary simulation command-and-control frameworks—predominantly Cobalt Strike Beacons and Brute Ratel C4 Badgers—enabling high-speed operational flexibility.
key_techniques: T1059.001 - Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
T1071.001 - Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
stages.procedures: Qakbot downloads and executes secondary payloads via PowerShell encoded stagers or reflective DLL injection into target processes (`svchost.exe`, `rundll32.exe`). Cobalt Strike Beacons and Brute Ratel Badgers communicate out to external infrastructure using custom Malleable C2 profiles that mimic legitimate web traffic (e.g. jQuery, Microsoft update headers).
stages.infrastructure_c2: Attacker-managed VPS infrastructure hosting Cobalt Strike team servers and Brute Ratel C4 listeners over HTTPS/TLS.

stages.stage_name: Credential Dumping and Rapid Lateral Movement to Domain Controllers
stages.description: Operators extract plaintext credentials, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets from memory. With elevated credentials, threat actors achieve Domain Admin privileges (routinely within 2 hours of initial access) and traverse laterally across critical network servers and domain controllers.
key_techniques: T1003.001 - OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory
T1021.001 - Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
T1021.002 - Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
stages.procedures: LSASS process memory is dumped using Mimikatz (`sekurlsa::logonpasswords`) or Sysinternals ProcDump to steal domain credentials. Attackers pivot laterally using PsExec (`psexec.exe -accepteula \\<target_ip> -u <domain>\<admin> -p <password> -s cmd.exe`), WMI (`wmic /node:<target_ip> process call create ...`), and Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) directly to domain controllers and key file servers.
stages.infrastructure_c2: Internal SMB named-pipe Beacons pivoting traffic to external egress Beacon nodes.

stages.stage_name: Environmental Sabotage, Defense Impairment, and DNS Service Disruption
stages.description: Prior to ransomware execution, the actors conduct targeted environmental sabotage to cripple incident response and recovery. They delete volume shadow copies, stop security services, and deliberately stop and disable DNS services across domain controllers to blind defenders and cut off name resolution.
key_techniques: T1562.001 - Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
stages.procedures: Attackers inhibit system recovery by executing: `vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet`, `wbadmin delete catalog -quiet`, and `bcdedit /set {default} bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures & bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled no`. Security agent services and antivirus software are terminated via `sc.exe stop` and registry tampering. Furthermore, the operators disable DNS services (`sc config "DNS" start=disabled` and `net stop "DNS Server"`) to lock responders out and prevent centralized remediation.
stages.infrastructure_c2: Batch execution scripts staged across domain controllers and pushed via PsExec.

stages.stage_name: Data Exfiltration and Enterprise-Wide Black Basta Ransomware Deployment
stages.description: Sensitive corporate files are staged and exfiltrated to cloud storage to support double-extortion. Black Basta ransomware binaries are then pushed across all accessible domain endpoints via PsExec or WMI, rapidly encrypting files, modifying system wallpapers, and dropping ransom notes.
key_techniques: T1567.002 - Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
stages.procedures: Sensitive corporate data is packaged and exfiltrated using Rclone to cloud providers (e.g., Mega, Wasabi). The Black Basta ransomware executable is copied to admin shares (`\\<target>\admin$\`) or `C:\Windows\Temp\` and executed via PsExec (`psexec.exe @hosts.txt -u <domain>\<admin> -p <pass> -s -d C:\Windows\Temp\basta.exe`). Files are encrypted with ChaCha20 and RSA-4096, appended with the `.basta` extension, `readme.txt` notes are dropped in each folder, and `HKCU\Control Panel\Desktop\Wallpaper` is modified to display the ransom announcement.
stages.infrastructure_c2: Black Basta Tor onion dark web leak and extortion portal.

mitre_attack_mappings.procedure_description: Delivering malicious ZIP files containing ISO/IMG disk images disguised as invoices or business correspondence via hijacked email threads.
Sending hyperlinks inside hijacked email conversations leading to external download staging sites hosting password-protected archive files.
Victim mounts disk image container and double-clicks disguised shortcut (.lnk) file or batch script to begin payload unpacking.
Invoking rundll32.exe with exported functions (e.g. `Wind` or `DllRegisterServer`) to execute packed Qakbot loader DLLs.
Executing encoded PowerShell commands to download and reflectively load secondary C2 stagers into memory.
Creating scheduled tasks via schtasks.exe to execute Qakbot DLLs periodically and maintain foothold upon reboot.

mitre_attack_mappings.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
mitre_attack_mappings.procedure_description: Adding autorun registry keys in HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run pointing to dropped loader binaries.
Injecting unpacked Qakbot and Cobalt Strike payload code into spawned wermgr.exe, explorer.exe, or svchost.exe processes.

mitre_attack_mappings.technique_name: Subversion of Stream Attributes: Mark-of-the-Web Bypass
mitre_attack_mappings.procedure_description: Encapsulating payloads inside ISO and IMG disk containers so extracted child files do not inherit the Zone.Identifier MotW stream.

mitre_attack_mappings.technique_name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
mitre_attack_mappings.procedure_description: Disabling Windows Defender, altering registry security keys, and stopping endpoint detection services.
Executing `net group "Domain Admins" /domain` and querying Active Directory via AdFind to map privileged user accounts.
Querying local operating system configuration, architecture, and patch level via native CLI tools (`whoami /all`, `systeminfo`).
Running `ipconfig /all`, `route print`, and `arp -a` to identify network interfaces, subnets, and neighboring devices.
Querying domain controllers and trust topologies using `nltest /dclist:<domain>` and `nltest /domain_trusts`.
Dumping LSASS process memory via Mimikatz (`sekurlsa::logonpasswords`) or ProcDump to obtain cleartext credentials and NTLM hashes.
Staging ransomware executables and malicious scripts onto remote systems via administrative shares (`ADMIN$`, `C$`).
Using PsExec to spawn remote services and execute commands with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges across domain systems.
Executing remote commands and launching payloads on network endpoints via `wmic /node:<target> process call create`.
Communicating with external C2 servers over HTTPS using custom Malleable C2 HTTP request profiles.

mitre_attack_mappings.technique_name: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
mitre_attack_mappings.procedure_description: Exfiltrating sensitive intellectual property, finance files, and databases using Rclone to cloud storage targets prior to encryption.
Deleting volume shadow copies with `vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet` and deleting Windows backup catalogs.
Stopping database, hypervisor, and critical system services (including stopping DNS Server) to unlock files and cause operational disruption.
Disabling the Windows DNS Server service (`sc config "DNS" start=disabled`) across domain controllers to knock out name resolution network-wide.
Encrypting files across network drives and local partitions using ChaCha20 and RSA-4096, appending the `.basta` extension.
Overwriting desktop background wallpapers with ransom warning graphics and dropping `readme.txt` across all directories.

detection_rules: Sigma: Suspicious Rundll32 Execution Calling Wind/DllRegisterServer Export
Sigma: Service Configuration Tampering Disabling Windows DNS Server Service
Sigma: Volume Shadow Copy Deletion via Vssadmin/WMIC/Bcdedit
Sigma: PsExec Lateral Movement Spawning Processes Under Admin Shares
Sigma: Mass File Renaming With .basta Extension and Ransom Note Drop

summary: This intrusion chain demonstrates a fast-moving, high-impact attack where threat actors leverage thread-hijacked phishing emails delivering ISO disk images to infect endpoints with Qakbot. Once established, Qakbot injects into trusted system processes, performs automated Active Directory discovery, and downloads secondary post-exploitation C2 frameworks (Cobalt Strike and Brute Ratel). Threat actors rapidly dump LSASS credentials, achieve Domain Administrator privileges in under two hours, and traverse laterally via PsExec, WMI, and RDP. Before deploying ransomware, the operators impair defensive visibility and cause network chaos by destroying backups and deliberately disabling DNS services on domain controllers. The attack culminates in enterprise-wide deployment of Black Basta ransomware and double extortion within 12 to 24 hours of initial access.
emulation_utility:
This intrusion chain represents a premier candidate for adversary emulation engineering due to its multi-layered, modern modular architecture combining commodity initial access loaders, advanced post-exploitation C2, living-off-the-land lateral movement, and destructive environmental sabotage. To construct an adversary emulation playbook from this intelligence:
1. Phase 1 (Initial Access & MotW Bypass): Emulate user-driven mounting of an ISO/IMG containing an LNK that launches a non-malicious DLL via rundll32.exe, validating EDR Mark-of-the-Web telemetry and process creation monitoring.
2. Phase 2 (Process Injection & Persistence): Emulate process injection from the loader into wermgr.exe or svchost.exe using process hollowing/APC injection, alongside scheduled task persistence creation.
3. Phase 3 (Discovery & Staging): Execute scripted discovery commands (whoami, net view, nltest, AdFind queries) to evaluate behavioral anomaly detections on rapid host and domain profiling.
4. Phase 4 (Privilege Escalation & LSASS Dumping): Emulate credential extraction using memory dumping techniques against LSASS (e.g. Sysinternals ProcDump or safe mimikatz alternatives) to test credential theft monitoring.
5. Phase 5 (Lateral Movement): Execute lateral service creation and command dispatch using PsExec/SMB and WMI to simulate pivoting to simulated domain controller targets.
6. Phase 6 (Environmental Sabotage): Safely test defense impairment by executing non-destructive service configuration queries and shadow copy enumeration, while evaluating alerting on commands attempting to disable DNS (`sc config DNS start=disabled`).
7. Phase 7 (Ransomware Canary Emulation): Deploy a safe ransomware simulator or canary script that creates benign test files, simulates file renaming with .basta extensions, and sets canary wallpaper changes to measure file integrity monitoring and automated endpoint response.
